passages.happening:
The book opens with a date and a promise kept. ‘In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send a proclamation throughout his kingdom and to put it in writing as follows’ (verse 1).

Then comes the proclamation itself. The king says that ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah’ (verse 2). Any of the LORD's people may go up to Jerusalem and build the house of the LORD, ‘the God of Israel; He is the God who is in Jerusalem’ (verse 3).

And those who stay behind are to help the ones who go, with silver and gold, goods and livestock, ‘along with a freewill offering for the house of God in Jerusalem’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The first year of Cyrus means his first year as king over Babylon. Cyrus captured Babylon in October 539 BC, so his decree belongs to 539 or 538 BC. About fifty years had passed since the Babylonians burned Jerusalem and its temple, in 587 or 586 BC, and carried the people of Judah away.

Persian kings often let peoples whom earlier empires had deported go home and restore their temples. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay cylinder found at Babylon in 1879 and now in the British Museum, describes Cyrus returning the images of gods to their sanctuaries and gathering their peoples back to their homes. It does not mention the Jews, and it concerns cities in Mesopotamia, but it shows the kind of decree this chapter describes. A second, plainer form of Cyrus's order, kept as an archive record in Aramaic, appears in 6:3-5.

The decree calls the LORD ‘the God of heaven’ (verse 2). That title was used in the Persian period for the supreme god, and it appears often in Ezra and Nehemiah. Persian kings were used to honoring the gods of their subject peoples, and it would be natural for a decree for the Jews to be written in words the Jews themselves would use.

A first hearer would also catch the word stirred. In Hebrew it is the verb for waking someone from sleep. The LORD stirs the spirit of a foreign king here, and four verses later he stirs ordinary families. Pagan king and faithful Jew alike move because God moves them.
passages.later:
The same decree closes 2 Chronicles, in the same words (2 Chronicles 36:22-23). So the two books join like links in a chain: the story of Israel's kings ends in exile, and the story of the return begins with a foreign king.

The prophet whose word is kept had written to the exiles in Babylon, “When Babylon’s seventy years are complete, I will attend to you and confirm My promise to restore you to this place” (Jeremiah 29:10). In Isaiah, the LORD calls the Persian king by name: ‘This is what the LORD says to Cyrus His anointed’ (Isaiah 45:1). He adds, ‘I call you by name; I have given you a title of honor, though you have not known Me’ (Isaiah 45:4).
passages.hard:
Why would a Persian king call the LORD the God who appointed him to build a temple?

Some readers find it unlikely that Cyrus would say that the LORD had given him all the kingdoms of the earth. But the Cyrus Cylinder shows the same pattern in Babylon, where Cyrus says that the Babylonian god Marduk chose him and called him to rule. Persian kings routinely honored the gods of their subjects, and an official decree for one people was often drafted with the help of members of that people, in their own religious language.

So the wording does not mean that Cyrus became a worshiper of the LORD. It means that he was willing to present himself as the chosen servant of Judah's God, as he presented himself as the chosen servant of other gods elsewhere.

Some scholars think the Hebrew form of the decree has been shaped by the Jewish writer, since the Aramaic record in 6:3-5 is plainer. Others argue that both are true forms of one decree, a public proclamation and an archive note. Either way, the book's point stands. It was the LORD who stirred Cyrus, whatever Cyrus thought he was doing.
passages.asks: God kept his promise through a king who did not know him. Ask where you have seen good things begin through people who never meant to serve God. And ask what promise of God you are still waiting to see kept, and what it would take to act on it while the circumstances still look bleak.

passages.t: The people go, and the vessels come home
passages.happening:
The family heads of Judah and Benjamin, with the priests and Levites, get ready to go up and rebuild the house of the LORD in Jerusalem: ‘everyone whose spirit God had stirred’ (verse 5). Their neighbors help them ‘with articles of silver and gold, with goods and livestock, and with valuables’ (verse 6), besides all their freewill offerings.

‘King Cyrus also brought out the articles belonging to the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the temple of his gods’ (verse 7). The royal treasurer, Mithredath, counts them out to Sheshbazzar, ‘the prince of Judah’ (verse 8).

The chapter lists them: gold dishes, silver dishes, silver utensils, gold bowls, silver bowls and other articles. ‘In all, there were 5,400 gold and silver articles’ (verse 11). Sheshbazzar brings them all when the exiles go up from Babylon to Jerusalem.
passages.hearers:
Not everyone was stirred. Many Jews had settled in Babylonia, as Jeremiah had told them to, and most of them stayed. Those who went were the ones whose spirit God had moved, and the rest helped them on their way.

When Israel left Egypt, the Egyptians gave them articles of silver and gold. Here, too, the neighbors send the travelers off loaded with gifts, and a first hearer would hear an echo of that first rescue.

Ancient conquerors carried off the images and sacred objects of the peoples they defeated and set them in their own temples, as a public sign that their gods had won. Israel had no image of its God, so Nebuchadnezzar took the temple's vessels instead and set them in the temple of his gods (verse 7). Giving them back was more than returning property. It undid the shame, and it said that the house of Israel's God would stand again.

Sheshbazzar is a figure of some mystery. The title prince honors him without calling him king, which suits a people under Persian rule, and in 5:14 he is called governor. Some identify him with Zerubbabel, who leads the returnees in the next chapters. Others link him with Shenazzar, a son of King Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:18). Others see him as an official whom Persia appointed to lead the first group before Zerubbabel took over.

The people who went up were called the golah, the exile (verse 11). The word became a name for the returned community: people defined by having been carried away, and by God bringing them back.
passages.later:
When Israel left Egypt, the people ‘asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing’ (Exodus 12:35).

The vessels have a long story in the Bible. Second Kings tells how the Babylonians carried them off when Jerusalem fell (2 Kings 25:13-15). The book of Daniel tells of Belshazzar drinking from them at his feast: ‘Thus they brought in the gold vessels that had been taken from the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem’ (Daniel 5:3). Here they come home.

And a psalm remembers what the homecoming felt like: ‘When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers’ (Psalm 126:1).
passages.hard:
The numbers in verses 9 to 11 do not add up. The articles listed come to 2,499, but verse 11 gives a total of 5,400, and the Greek book of 1 Esdras has different figures again.

The gap probably comes from copying. Numbers were easily confused in ancient manuscripts. Or the total may include items that were not listed one by one. The list's purpose is plain on any reading: what was taken was counted, and what was counted came home.
passages.asks: The vessels taken as trophies came back to their proper place. Ask what in your own life has been taken or misused, and what it would look like for it to be returned to its proper use. And ask whether, like those neighbors, you have helped someone else go where God was calling them.
